Potential techniques: equal weight and longer windows

beats.text: Here is the setup. A person's foot is strapped to a pedal, with the pedal's axis lined up with the ankle. The pedal belongs to a dynamometer: a machine that holds the ankle at a chosen angle, and measures the twisting force, the torque, that the person applies to it. Torque is measured in newton metres.

beats.vis: Four electrode dots appear on the leg in their colours: GM and GL (the two bulges of the calf), soleus (lower, under them), TA (front of the shin). Side labels: "calf: pushes the toes down", "shin: pulls the toes up".
beats.text: On the leg sit four surface electrodes. They record the EMG, short for electromyography: the tiny electrical signal a muscle gives off when it is told to contract. Three are on the calf: the two bulges of the calf muscle, called GM and GL, and the soleus underneath them. These three push the toes down. The fourth sits on the shin: the tibialis anterior, or TA. It pulls the toes up.

beats.vis: The pedal rotates through eight settings, each drawn in the angle colour ramp, labelled with EG's session-1 angles in rad (−0.739 … +0.247). Two arrows: "negative = toes down (plantarflexion)", "positive = toes up (dorsiflexion)". The word "position" appears under the eight settings. EG's peak torques per position as small bars under each setting (4 → 40 Nm), toes-down labelled "weak", toes-up "strong".
beats.text: The angle is fixed during a recording, but it changes between recordings, to eight different settings. We call each setting a position. Angles are in radians. Negative means toes down, which is called plantarflexion. Positive means toes up, called dorsiflexion. For EG, the eight positions run from about minus 0.74 to plus 0.25 radians. With the toes down, the calf can push the least, so we call those the weak positions. With the toes up, people push hardest: the strong positions.

beats.text: We have recordings from six people, and we only use their codes. Each was recorded in two sessions, during the same visit. According to our audit notes, the electrodes stayed on in between. The files call the sessions test and retest; we will call them session 1 and session 2. The whole project rests on one question: if a model learns from session 1, can it predict session 2?

beats.text: There are three kinds of trial. First, maximum-effort trials, called MVC: thirty seconds each, recorded once at the start of the visit. The baseline does not use them. Then, in each session, passive and active trials. A passive trial begins with twenty to thirty seconds where the person relaxes and the machine holds the foot still. What follows is not a relaxed hold, and the code has to cut it away. And the active trials are the ones we model: ninety seconds of repeated pushes, one trial per position, so eight per session.

beats.vis: EG session-1 active trial at −0.038 rad, full 89 s at 100 Hz: torque (white) with 22 downward dips; angle (light grey) drawn above as a flat line with the label "moves by a few mrad". Counter "22 pushes". Label: "size of a push = how deep the dip goes".
beats.text: This is one active trial: EG at minus 0.04 radians. On this machine, a calf push shows up as negative torque, so each push is a dip. There are twenty-two of them in ninety seconds. When we talk about how strong a push is, we mean how deep the dip goes. On top, the angle is flat: the pedal barely moves, by only a few thousandths of a radian. These are called isometric contractions: the muscles work, but the joint does not move.

beats.vis: Zoom into 2 s of the same trial at 1 kHz: four raw EMG traces (GM, GL, soleus, TA in their colours) stacked under the torque. A bracket on one push: "bigger push → bigger scribble". Small label "1 sample = 1 recorded value; 1,000 per second".
beats.text: And this is the raw EMG behind two seconds of that trial. It is recorded as a thousand values per second, and each value is called a sample. The EMG looks like noise, because it is the sum of many tiny electrical spikes. What matters is its size: push harder, and the scribble gets bigger. Turning that scribble into a smooth measure of effort is the first step of the pipeline, the chain of steps from raw signals to a prediction.

beats.vis: Stacked cartoon of the measured torque = "active (muscles contracting)" + "passive (relaxed reading)". An ankle drawing with a spring across it ("stretched tendons, muscles, skin") and a small weight icon on the foot ("weight of the foot and pedal"). With the person relaxed, the measured torque is not zero: the passive part remains.
beats.text: Before we touch the EMG, we need to be precise about what the model has to predict. The sensor at the pedal measures the total torque. Part of that comes from the muscles contracting. We call it the active torque. But some torque is there even when the person is completely relaxed. Stretched tendons, muscles and skin pull back, a bit like a rubber band, and the weight of the foot and the pedal adds to it. We call that whole relaxed reading the passive torque.

beats.text: Where does the passive torque come from? From the start of the passive trials. The machine holds the relaxed foot still, and the code takes the average torque over that hold: roughly one number per position. Join those numbers with straight lines, and you get the passive table: passive torque against angle. Between two measured angles, the code reads along the line. Each session gets its own table, built from its own passive trials.

beats.text: Then, for every sample of an active trial, the code looks up the passive torque at the measured angle, and subtracts it. Because the angle barely moves, that value is almost constant. For EG at this position, it is about minus 3.5 newton metres in session 1. In session 2 it is minus 2.6. What remains is the target: the active torque.

beats.text: A question we get a lot: does the network predict the total torque? No. It outputs the active torque directly. Nothing is added back, and the total torque is never predicted. The ground truth, which we will also call the answer key, is built the same way: the torque measured in session 2, minus session 2's own passive table. One detail: for every score in this video, that table is rebuilt from the still, relaxed holds only. That changes nothing for five people, and changes JM's table, which we will come back to.

beats.text: Now, the EMG. Each electrode gives one signal, which we call a channel. Every channel goes through the same six steps, shown along the top. We will follow three seconds of the soleus channel through each one.

beats.vis: Step 1: the raw piece with a dashed line at its average; the trace shifts so the line sits at zero.
beats.text: Step one: remove the average. The amplifier can add a small constant level to the signal, so the code subtracts the average of the whole trial. The signal is now centred on zero.
beats.src: emg_envelope.py:28-32 (whole-trial mean); x02 piece_demeaned.

beats.vis: Step 2: a small gain-versus-frequency plot with the 30–300 Hz band shaded ("kept"); below 30 Hz labelled "cable and skin movement". The piece after band-pass replaces the raw piece. Small tag: "same band as Zhang et al. 2022".
beats.text: Step two: a band-pass filter, from 30 to 300 hertz. Think of it as a sieve for wiggle speeds. Very slow wiggles are where cable and skin movement shows up. Most of the muscle's signal sits in the middle range, so the code keeps 30 to 300 hertz, the same band as one of the papers we built on. Some genuine muscle signal above 300 hertz is thrown away, too.
beats.src: 4th-order Butterworth 30–300 Hz (facts_x02 bp, order); emg_envelope.py:7, 29-30; Zhang 2022 p.601 (30–300 Hz); Ranaldi 2022 p4 (25–450 Hz); x02 gain_bp, piece_band.

beats.vis: Step 3: negative parts of the trace flip upward (animated mirror at zero).
beats.text: Step three: rectify. The signal swings positive and negative, but the sign carries no information about effort. Only the size does. So every negative value is flipped to positive.
beats.src: x02 piece_rect.

beats.vis: Step 4: a smooth curve is drawn through the rectified spikes: the envelope (soleus colour, thick). Label "envelope". Small inset of the 2 Hz low-pass gain curve.
beats.text: Step four: a low-pass filter at 2 hertz. It keeps only slow changes, and draws a smooth curve through the rectified spikes. That curve is called the envelope. It rises when the muscle works harder, and falls when it relaxes. This is the signal the network will actually see.
beats.src: facts_x02 lp 2.0; x02 piece_env, gain_lp.

beats.vis: The 2 Hz filter's weighting curve centred on "now", reaching both into the past and the future; the part to the right of "now" is shaded and labelled "future". Badge: "forward + backward → no delay, but it reaches about 0.4 s into the future (a faint tail to ≈ 0.9 s) → offline only".
beats.text: A detail that matters later. Both filters are run forwards over the whole trial, and then backwards. That cancels the delay a filter normally adds. But it also means the envelope at any moment is partly built from the next few tenths of a second. That is fine for analysing recordings. A real-time device could not do it. So every result in this video is an offline result.

beats.text: Step five. The first second of each trial is cut off. The code's comment says this removes a start-up effect of the filters. Oddly, the end of the trial, where the same kind of effect can appear, is not trimmed.

So that the network sees comparable numbers, the baseline divides each channel by the single largest value it reached anywhere in session 1's eight active trials. Across session 1, every channel now tops out at one. A single trial, like this one, usually stays well below it.

For the same push, a muscle's signal can come out smaller, or larger, in session 2, and the model has no way of knowing. And this happens. Each bar here is session 2's EMG size per newton metre of push, divided by session 1's. One would mean no change. For JM at minus 0.36 radians, GM and the soleus come out at only about a third of their session-1 size. GL drops less, to about four fifths.

The next 1,778, about the last eighteen seconds, are held back for validation. Because of rounding, the very last window of each trial is not used at all.

beats.text: The bigger point is this. Validation is just the end of the same trials, a few seconds later: the same moment of the visit, the same electrode contact, the same passive table, the same angle for each trial. So validation can tell us whether the model fits session 1. It cannot tell us anything about what changes between sessions. Hold on to that, because it explains a lot.

beats.text: Now the network itself, from far away. It is a neural network called an LSTM, short for long short-term memory, a type built for sequences. It reads the window one time step at a time, oldest first, and keeps a small memory that it updates at every step. The baseline stacks two of these layers. Each has a memory of just eight numbers. After them comes a single output: the predicted active torque, in newton metres. In total, the network has 1,001 adjustable numbers, called weights.
beats.src: models/lstm.py:17-24; n_params 1001 in all 60 X00 jsons.

beats.vis: Animation: the 20 columns of the window enter the first layer one at a time; its 8 memory squares change brightness at each step and pass a sequence to the second layer; after the 20th step the second layer's memory feeds one output number that pops out.
beats.text: You can picture it like reading a sentence, word by word. After each word, you update your sense of what is going on. After the twentieth time step, the network's memory is boiled down into one number. That is the prediction for that window.
beats.src: LSTM(8, return_sequences) → LSTM(8) → Dense(1).

beats.vis: After the output pops out, the 8 memory squares fade to blank; the next window (from a different trial and time, since batches are shuffled) slides in and starts from blank squares. Label: "memory starts empty for every window: the network sees 0.2 s, nothing else".
beats.text: An important detail: that memory starts empty for every window. Nothing is carried over from one window to the next, and since the windows are shuffled, the network would not even see them in order. Each prediction is made from those twenty time steps, a fifth of a second, and nothing else.
beats.src: models/lstm.py (Keras LSTM, stateful=False default); build_windows makes independent windows; model.fit(shuffle=True).

beats.vis: Two dropout boxes appear: one after each LSTM layer (the second just before the output). During "training", about 30 % of the signals leaving each layer flicker off at random, different ones every batch; the rest brighten slightly ("scaled up"). A switch flips to "checking or predicting" and everything stays on.
beats.text: After each of the two layers sits dropout, set to 0.3. During training, on every batch, each signal leaving that layer has a thirty percent chance of being switched off, and the rest are scaled up to make up for it. So the network cannot rely on any single path, which pushes it towards sturdier solutions. When the model is checked, or used for prediction, dropout is turned off, and everything is used.

beats.vis: Three bars for "memory cells per layer": ours 8, Zhang et al. 2022: 50, Kim et al. 2020: 200.
beats.text: For scale: eight memory cells is tiny. The LSTM papers we built on used fifty, and two hundred. We will come back to whether size matters.
beats.src: Zhang 2022 p.602 (50 units, 2–4 layers); Kim 2020 p.3820 (200 hidden units).

beats.vis: One window → prediction vs answer; the error drawn as a vertical gap, then squared (a square whose side is the gap). Three squares: "miss 1 → cost 1", "miss 2 → cost 4", "miss 3 → cost 9". Many squares averaged into one number: "loss = mean squared error (Nm²)".
beats.text: Training means finding values for those 1,001 weights that make the predictions good. "Good" is measured by the loss. For each window, take the error, the prediction minus the answer, and square it. A miss of one costs one. A miss of two costs four. A miss of three costs nine. Then average over many windows. This is the mean squared error, in newton metres squared. Squaring means a big miss costs far more than a small one.
beats.src: loss 'mse' (config.py:73-79).

beats.vis: One training step: 8 windows drawn at random from the fit set (from different trials and times) → 8 predictions → loss → small arrows nudge all the weights. Labels: "batch = 8 windows", "optimiser: Nadam (a variant of Adam)", "learning rate (step size) 0.003".
beats.text: One training step works like this. Pick eight windows at random from the fit set. That group of eight is called a batch. Predict all eight, measure the loss, and nudge every weight a little, in the direction that would have made the loss smaller. The rule that decides the nudge is called the optimiser. Here it is Nadam, a variant of the well-known Adam. And the size of the nudge is set by the learning rate: 0.003.
beats.src: Nadam(lr 0.003), batch 8, shuffle=True (config.py:73-79; training/__init__.py:122-147).

beats.vis: A progress bar fills through 56,896 fit windows, eight at a time: "7,112 steps = 1 epoch = every fit window seen once". Small note: "7,112 again: 8 trials and batches of 8". At its end, a "quiz" stamp on the validation set: "validation error checked · no learning".
beats.text: There are 56,896 fit windows, and we take eight at a time. Do that 7,112 times, and every fit window has been seen once. That is one epoch: one full pass through the training data. The same 7,112 as the windows per trial is just a coincidence of the arithmetic: eight trials, and batches of eight. At the end of each epoch, the model is checked on the validation windows. No learning happens there. It is just a quiz.

beats.vis: Truth and prediction for a few seconds; vertical error bars between them; their absolute lengths average into "MAE = average size of the miss (Nm)".
beats.text: The simplest score is the mean absolute error, MAE: the average size of the miss, in newton metres. It is easy to read. An MAE of 0.5 means the prediction is typically half a newton metre off.
beats.src: evaluation/metrics.py; presentation_metrics.py:81-88.

beats.vis: The truth with a flat dashed line at its own average: "lazy guess". Squared errors of the lazy guess (big squares) next to those of the model (small squares). Formula in words: "R² = 1 − (sum of model's squared errors ÷ sum of lazy guess's squared errors)". A scale: 1 = perfect · 0 = no better than the flat line · below 0 = worse than the flat line. Small warning tag on the flat line: "knows the true average of this very trial".
beats.text: The score we report most is R². It compares the model with a lazy guess: a flat line at the trial's own average torque. Add up the model's squared errors. Add up the lazy guess's squared errors. Divide the first by the second, and take that away from one. If the model is perfect, R² is one. If it is no better than the flat line, zero. And if it is worse than the flat line, it goes negative. Note that this lazy guess is handed the true average of the very trial being scored, which the model never sees. So zero does not mean no skill.
beats.src: metrics.py:13-77 (R² = 1 − SS_res/SS_tot with the local mean, per position).

beats.vis: The same error band (same size in Nm) drawn twice: over a strong position with big swings (the lazy guess is far off → R² ≈ 0.99) and over a toes-down position with small swings (the lazy guess is already close → R² collapses).
beats.text: Here is the catch. The lazy guess is very good when the torque hardly moves, and very bad when it swings a lot. So the same error in newton metres can give an excellent R² at a strong position, and a terrible one at a weak position. R² is a score relative to how much there was to predict.

beats.vis: Left: one big badge "the old code's R², all 8 positions pooled · YES: 0.97–0.98 in all 10 seeds". Right: YES's eight per-position R² bars for the same runs, the −0.486 bar plunging below zero ("−2.0 to 0.01"). Footer: "pooled, typical run: ≈ 0.94–0.99 per person".

Pooling counts the big differences between strong and weak positions as explained, so a failure at one weak position barely moves it. That is why we score each position on its own.

The tell-tale sign is a gap: excellent on the data it trained on, and much worse on similar data it has not seen.

It shares everything specific to that moment of session 1: the electrode contact, the passive table, the angle of each trial. So if the model had learned session 1's quirks, validation could not tell. What we can say is that the big drop comes only with session 2. beats.text: The idea is simple. For each muscle, the code keeps a running estimate of two levels, looking only backwards in time. A floor, what the muscle reads when quiet: a low point of the last twenty seconds. And a top, what it reads during strong pushes: a high point of the last forty-five seconds. Every half second, both are updated, and the signal is rescaled so the floor maps to zero and the top to one. This is done to every trial, training trials included, so the network also learns on rescaled signals.

beats.text: A longer window is not cheating in itself: it still only looks backwards, and nothing from session 2 enters training. But picking any setting because it scored best on the test session is a softer problem, called selection bias. Nothing leaks into the model, but the reported score is optimistic, because the choice was fitted to that test.

beats.vis: Four paper cards: "Zhang et al. 2022 · LSTM · hip, knee, ankle torque in walking, jumps, squats"; "Kim et al. 2020 · LSTM · wrist angle and torque"; "Zhang et al. 2019 · high-density EMG · elbow force"; "Ranaldi et al. 2022 · how to compute the EMG envelope". Small note on the last: "file name says 'Renaldi'".
beats.text: Finally, the four papers our approach was based on. Two train LSTMs: Zhang and colleagues, 2022, predicting hip, knee and ankle torques, and Kim and colleagues, 2020, predicting wrist angle and torque. Two are about EMG processing: Zhang and colleagues, 2019, on high-density EMG for elbow force, and Ranaldi and colleagues, 2022, on how the envelope is computed.
beats.src: paper citations (scratchpad wf1 paper_*.md; PDFs).

beats.vis: One row at a time at large size (earlier rows collapse to one-word labels down the left). Difference 1, "sessions": ours "2 sessions: learn one, test the other"; Kim 2020 "a new 80 s phase after a 2-min break"; Zhang 2022 "held-back part of the same recordings, new people, new movements"; Zhang 2019 "other repetitions of the same trial"; Ranaldi "no model". The row glows.
beats.text: Difference one, the most important: none of the four tests on a separate session. Kim comes closest, testing on a new eighty-second phase after a two-minute break. The others test on held-back parts of the same recordings, or, in Zhang 2022, also on new people and movements. Our two sessions are in the same visit too, but the EMG size and the passive levels still shift between them, and none of the papers studies that shift. So we should not expect to match their scores.
beats.src: Zhang 2022 pp.601-603; Kim 2020 p.3821 (80 s phases, 2-min breaks); Zhang 2019 p.1925 (within one trial); Ranaldi §2 (no model).

beats.vis: Difference 2, "target": ours "active = measured − passive table"; Zhang 2022 "total joint torque (motion capture + force plates)"; Kim 2020 "measured net torque"; Zhang 2019 "total force"; Ranaldi "no model".
beats.text: Difference two: none subtracts a passive torque. The three modelling papers predict the total torque, or force, directly. Our subtraction, which brings the passive table and its offsets into the answer key, is our own design choice. The papers neither support it nor rule it out.
beats.src: Zhang 2022 p.601 (inverse dynamics); Kim 2020 p.3820 (net torque); Zhang 2019 p.1923 (total force); Ranaldi (no model).

beats.vis: Difference 3, "score": ours "R² per position (punishes offsets)"; Zhang 2022 "error per kg · error ÷ torque range"; Kim 2020 "variance accounted for (formula not given; usually ignores offsets)"; Ranaldi "correlation at the best lag (ignores offset and scale) + error after normalising"; Zhang 2019 (next beat).
beats.text: Difference three: how performance is scored. Zhang 2022 reports the error per kilogram of body mass, and as a fraction of the torque range. Kim reports the variance accounted for, which usually ignores a constant offset. Ranaldi mainly uses correlation at the best time lag, which ignores both offset and scale.
beats.src: Zhang 2022 p.604; Kim 2020 p.3822 (VAF, formula not given); Ranaldi §2.3.

beats.vis: Two notes in the score row: Kim 2020 "torque not scored in the zero-resistance condition: mostly noise"; Zhang 2019 "R² per force level: best method 0.93 at 60 % of maximum effort → 0.84 at 20 %".
beats.text: Two more points on scoring. Kim did not score torque at all in the condition where it was meant to be zero, because what remained was mostly noise. Our toes-down positions are a milder version of that problem: real pushes, but small. And Zhang 2019 scored each force level separately, like our per-position R², and found R² falling as the force gets weaker, for every method: their best went from 0.93 at 60 percent of maximum effort, to 0.84 at 20 percent.
beats.src: Kim 2020 p.3822 (CASE 1 torque not evaluated); Zhang 2019 p.1926 (method 1 R² 0.932 / 0.901 / 0.840).

beats.vis: Difference 4, "network": ours "2 layers × 8 cells · dropout 0.3 · batch 8 · 0.2 s windows"; Zhang 2022 "2–4 layers × 50 cells · dropout 0.4 · batch 50 · input slices of only 5 time steps"; Kim 2020 "1 layer × 200 cells · dropout 0.5 · one participant: shuffling training data in short chunks hurt, mostly for the angle"; Zhang 2019 "a cubic polynomial, 4 numbers, fitted per person and force level".
beats.text: Difference four: the network. Zhang 2022 used two to four layers of fifty cells, Kim one layer of two hundred; ours has two layers of eight. Zhang 2022 fed even shorter input slices than ours, five time steps each. Kim found, for one participant, that shuffling the training data in chunks of five seconds or less made predictions worse, mostly for the angle, which hints that longer context helps. And Zhang 2019 reached an R² of 0.84 to 0.93 with a four-number polynomial, but fitted per person and force level, and tested on repeats of the same trial.
beats.src: Zhang 2022 p.602 (Fig. 2 caption: five time steps; 50 units; dropout 0.4; batch 50); Kim 2020 pp.3820-3823 (200 units, dropout 0.5; Table 2 subject 3, CASE 3); Zhang 2019 pp.1924-1926 (cubic polynomial; train on 1 of 5 segments).

beats.vis: Difference 5, "envelope": ours "30–300 Hz · rectify · 2 Hz"; Zhang 2022 "30–300 Hz · rectify · 6 Hz"; Zhang 2019 "20–400 Hz · cut-off tuned per person and force level: 1–3 Hz, most often 1 Hz, the lowest allowed"; Ranaldi "25–450 Hz + 50 Hz notch · slow smoothing (200–500 ms) scored highest on their correlation measure, which favours smooth envelopes; an adaptive envelope was comparable"; Kim "size (RMS) + frequency-shape features over 100 ms".
beats.text: Difference five: the EMG processing. Our band-pass matches Zhang 2022's, and our 2 hertz smoothing is in the usual range: Zhang 2022 used 6. Zhang 2019 tuned the smoothing per person and force level, and the best cut-off fell between 1 and 3 hertz, most often at 1, the lowest they allowed. Kim used different features: the signal's size, plus the shape of its frequency content. Unlike the size, that shape does not change when the whole signal is scaled, which could matter when the EMG changes size between sessions.
beats.src: Zhang 2022 p.601; Zhang 2019 p.1926, p.1929 (1–2.5 Hz at 20/40 %, 1–3 Hz at 60 %; 'left border of range as 1 Hz'); Ranaldi §2.2–3.3; Kim 2020 p.3820 (RMS + AR(6)); AR coefficients are unchanged by scaling (our observation).

beats.vis: Row "scaling": ours "÷ session-1 maximum, also applied to session 2"; Zhang 2022 "÷ maximum over all its trials (same recording as the test)"; Zhang 2019 "MVC only sets the target force levels"; Kim "none described"; Ranaldi "not described". Side note: "tried here earlier: ÷ MVC did worse than auto-gain".
beats.text: And scaling. A textbook answer is to divide the EMG by a maximum-effort contraction, but none of the four papers does. Zhang 2022 divides by the largest value over all its trials, so in a single-session study, the scale comes from the recording being tested. Zhang 2019 uses maximum effort only to set target forces, and Kim describes no scaling. So the papers say nothing about keeping a scale fixed across sessions. We did try maximum-effort scaling in an earlier round: it did worse than auto-gain, which fits with our MVC trials being recorded only once.
beats.src: Zhang 2022 p.601; Zhang 2019 p.1922; Kim (normalisation not stated); round2_report.md §7 (E10 0.887, E11 0.904 vs E03 0.925, batch-64 protocol); emg_norm.py:229-242.

beats.vis: Two-column verdict card. "Follows Zhang 2022 closely: LSTM on EMG envelopes + joint angle · same band-pass · squared-error loss · early stopping." "Our own choices: passive subtraction · 8 cells · applying session 1's scale to session 2 (a problem none of the papers faced)."
beats.text: So, does our method follow the literature? The honest answer has two halves. The general recipe follows Zhang 2022 closely: an LSTM on EMG envelopes and the joint angle, the same band-pass, a squared-error loss, early stopping. But the passive subtraction and the tiny network are our own choices. And applying session 1's scale to session 2 is a problem none of these papers faced, because none tested across sessions.
beats.src: Zhang 2022 pp.601-603; Kim 2020 p.3820 (inputs RMS + AR(6); outputs angle and torque).

beats.vis: Zhang 2022's transfer-learning result as two bars: "new person, no calibration: worst-case error ≈ 20 % of the range" → "pre-trained network, last layers replaced, retrained on that person's recordings (all layers gently adjusted): worst case ≈ 10 %".
beats.text: One result from Zhang 2022 stands out. For a new person, with no calibration, their error reached up to about twenty percent of the torque range in the worst movements, roughly double the worst within-person error, much like our drop to session 2. They then took the network trained on other people, replaced its last layers, and retrained it on recordings from the new person, gently adjusting the other layers too. That brought the worst-case error down to about ten percent: the closest thing in these papers to a fix for our problem, though it needs labelled data from the new person.
beats.src: Zhang 2022 p.602 §II-C, pp.604-606 (UW-inter 21 %, SW-inter 19.5 %; UWT 10.1 %, UBT 9.9 %; intra 8.7 %).

beats.vis: The whole pipeline as one line of icons: four EMG envelopes + angle → 0.2 s windows → small LSTM (2 × 8) → active torque (Nm). Below: "learn session 1 → test session 2".
beats.text: Let us sum up. The baseline turns four muscle signals into smooth envelopes. It cuts them, together with the angle, into windows a fifth of a second long, and trains a very small LSTM on session 1 to predict the active torque: the measured torque, minus a passive table. Then it is tested on session 2.

beats.vis: Summary bullets appearing one by one: "other positions: R² 0.97"; "toes-down: R² 0.77, though the error in Nm is smaller there"; "little to predict → offsets are over half of the lost score"; "offsets come from the answer key (YES) and from the model reacting to changed EMG (EG, IES)"; "not overfitting session 1: a session shift that validation cannot see"; "at toes-down, the R² depends heavily on the seed".
beats.text: At the thirty-six cells that are not toes-down, it works well, with an R² of 0.97. At toes-down it drops to 0.77, not because the errors are bigger in newton metres, but because there is so little to predict that small offsets are over half of the lost score. Those offsets come partly from the answer key, as for YES, and partly from the model reacting to changed session-2 EMG, as for EG and IES. Validation sees neither. The model is not overfitting session 1; it faces a different session. And at toes-down, R² depends heavily on the seed.

Our validation numbers already suggest that most of the gap is the session change; this would confirm it cleanly. Step nine: borrow Zhang 2022's idea of fine-tuning on a little labelled data from the new session, say the first fifteen to twenty seconds of each trial, a choice of ours, scoring only the rest, and report it as a separate method. beats.text: Some related ideas were already tried, in an earlier round, on three people, with faster settings. A straight-line correction fitted on the first seconds of each session-2 trial lifted the old pipeline from about 0.57 to 0.90 with half a minute of calibration, but added only one or two hundredths to the newer pipelines, and hurt them with five or ten seconds. A ridge regression trailed the LSTM clearly without auto-gain, and by about five hundredths with it. Pre-training on the other five people made things worse. Extra weight on toes-down did not help. And random EMG-size changes during training helped only without auto-gain.
